children: Prime Minister Narendra Modi has again urged Indians to avoid buying gold unless necessary, skip non-essential foreign travel and consider holding weddings in India, linking personal spending decisions to the country's economic resilience.

The appeal came in a video message from Bishkek on Tuesday, a day after official data showed India's economy grew 7.8% in the April-June quarter, beating expectations and keeping India among the fastest-growing major economies.
PM Modi said the strong growth came despite wars, global uncertainty and disrupted supply chains, but argued that India must continue strengthening its self-reliance.
“If you are going for leisure, you should not go. If you are getting married abroad, you should not do so. And if it is not necessary, you should not buy gold either,” PM Modi said.
The message is aimed at discretionary spending that sends money overseas, at a time when India's import bill and external vulnerabilities remain concerns.
Why does PM Modi want Indians to buy less gold?
India depends overwhelmingly on imported gold to meet domestic demand, making bullion one of the country's biggest import items after crude oil.
Every surge in gold demand therefore means greater foreign-exchange expenditure. This can add to the merchandise trade deficit and, when dollar demand is already elevated, put pressure on the rupee.
Gold imports have risen sharply this year.
Inbound shipments during the first four months of the financial year beginning April were more than 32% higher than a year earlier, reported
Bloomberg
. India's merchandise trade deficit also widened to nearly $32 billion in July, its highest level since January.
The issue is particularly significant because much of India's gold demand is driven by household savings, weddings, festivals and cultural practices rather than productive investment.
India is the world's second-largest bullion buyer, so even a modest shift in consumer demand can have a meaningful impact on the import bill.
Why does foreign travel matter?
PM Modi's appeal extends beyond physical goods.

When Indians travel overseas, their spending on hotels, restaurants, transport and entertainment largely benefits businesses outside India. Overseas weddings can involve an even larger outflow through expenditure on venues, accommodation, catering and travel.
The prime minister is therefore asking consumers to redirect some of this discretionary spending towards the domestic economy.
“If you go on holiday, go to a place in India. Wedding destinations can be in India. We should live the mantra of ‘wed in India’,” PM Modi said.
The broader argument is that money spent on an Indian holiday or wedding supports domestic businesses and jobs instead of contributing to foreign-exchange outflows.
Why is this important when GDP growth is strong?
The 7.8% growth recorded in the June quarter is a sign of economic resilience, but it does not eliminate India's exposure to external shocks.

India imports more than 88% of its crude-oil requirements, leaving the economy vulnerable to international energy prices. The continuing conflict in West Asia and uncertainty around the Strait of Hormuz have kept energy markets exposed to further disruptions.
A higher oil bill means India needs more foreign currency to pay for essential imports. Strong gold demand at the same time can compound that pressure.

PM Modi's argument is therefore not that one foreign holiday or one gold purchase threatens the economy. It is that millions of discretionary spending decisions can collectively affect the country's external finances.
This is not the first time the prime minister has asked Indians to cut discretionary spending overseas.

In May, amid heightened geopolitical tensions and concerns over crude prices, Modi urged people to avoid gold purchases for a year and postpone non-essential foreign travel. He also called for greater use of public transport and carpooling and encouraged measures to reduce fuel consumption.
The latest appeal revives that message even as India's growth numbers have strengthened.

PM Modi said global instability remains a concern, pointing to the disruption of supply chains since the Covid-19 pandemic. “The world is drowned in war. There is news of war all around. The world is surrounded by crises. The supply chain is completely disturbed,” he said. “Despite that, India is progressing at a fast pace," he noted.
Why is gold especially complicated right now?
Gold has become more attractive to investors amid geopolitical and economic uncertainty, making PM Modi's appeal harder to implement.
Bullion gained almost 10% in August, its biggest monthly increase since January. Spot gold was trading around $4,430 an ounce on Tuesday.
Higher global prices mean Indian consumers need to spend more rupees on imported bullion. Strong demand at elevated prices can therefore increase the country's import bill further.
At the same time, the
government is considering reducing import duties on gold and silver, although there has been no public indication that such a move is imminent.
That would create an interesting policy contrast - while the government may consider changing the tax burden on bullion, PM Modi is asking households to voluntarily reduce demand.
What is the larger ‘swadeshi’ push?
PM Modi's latest appeal is part of his broader push to encourage domestic consumption and self-reliance.

“The more we emphasise swadeshi, the more we emphasise self-reliance,” he said, expressing confidence that India could maintain its growth momentum and become a developed economy by the centenary of Independence.

title: Why PM Modi wants Indians to keep their gold, holidays and weddings in India
